newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Major faces uncomfortable Dublin weekend.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Major faces uncomfortable Dublin weekend.

text.p: There have been European Union summits that John Major enjoyed.

Freed from his domestic political straitjacket and the need to paper over splits between the quarrelling factions of the ruling Conservative party, Britain's prime minister often throws off his image as the grey man of politics and thrives in the role of statesman.
But not this weekend.
Major faces the seemingly impossible task of debating the future of Europe and keeping both pro-Europeans and so-called Eurosceptics in the ruling party happy.

His party's feuding over Europe is once again at fever pitch just seven months before the last possible date for an election and in the run-up to the Conservatives' last pre-poll party conference, starting on October 8.
The last thing Major needed was an extra EU summit to discuss highly controversial plans for the group's future.

But Britain's continental parners decided a review now underway of the bloc's treaties and institutions, known as the Inter-Governmental Conference (IGC), needed a push, so EU leaders will meet at Dublin Castle in Ireland on Sunday (Oct 5) to discuss it.
Few diplomats expect significant progress on contentious issues such as expanding majority voting in the EU to speed up decision-making, staunchly opposed by Britain.
But any sign of divisions between Britain and its partners will be seized on by Britain's press and relayed back home as a sign EU states are trying to push ahead with integration.

This will anger the Eurosceptics further, making it harder for Major to retain a semblance of control over his party as it goes into the election which will either end 17 years of Conservative rule or return the party for a record fifth term.
Some politicians believe the feuding is already out of hand.

With the opposition Labour party more than 20 points ahead in opinion polls, they say the battle is more about who will succeed Major when the party loses the election than about charting a sensible policy course for the next government.

Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, said last week: "I've no doubt whatsoever that this is the clearest sign of the pre-shocks of the earthquake that breaks the Tories up -- probably in defeat after the next election."

Even Major's close allies believe the split between those who want a constructive approach to Europe, led by Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke, and those who want looser links, led by former minister John Redwood, is a battle for succession.
"Too many people on both sides of this argument (Europe) aren't concentrating on... the election," said Conservative member of parliament Robert Hughes.

"They are simply positioning themselves for what is going to happen after the election, win or lose," said Hughes, on Major's campaign team when he took on Redwood last year in a party leadership battle designed to gag the Eurosceptics.
Major thought he had the ideal policy to bridge the gap when he negotiated an opt-out from a future single European currency in the Maastricht Treaty and adopted a "wait-and-see" approach.

But the Eurosceptics have wrung out of him the concession of a promise of a referendum before entry into a single currency and are now pushing for Major to rule out membership of a single currency in the life of the next five-year parliament.
The pro-Europeans have now begun to fight back.
Senior Conservatives, including former foreign ministers Douglas Hurd and Lord Howe, have brought together pro-European members of parliament in a new pressure group.

Major's slim chances of resolving the feuds have created renewed speculation that he may decide not to wait until April or May to call an election and instead call it in November if Labour's annual party conference this week hits problems.
